# Stream of Consciousness: A Thursday Afternoon

I'm sitting here trying to decide whether the blank page is terrifying or liberating. Maybe it's both. That's probably the most honest answer to most questions, isn't it? Both things at once. We're terrible at holding contradictions, though. We want everything to be simple: good or bad, right or wrong, love or hate. But life isn't a light switch. It's more like a dimmer, and we're all standing in rooms trying to figure out what the optimal brightness is.

I've been thinking lately about how we talk to ourselves. The internal monologue—that constant narrator we all have—is like having a critic permanently installed in your skull. Sometimes they're kind. Most times they're not. I wonder if everyone's inner voice is as much of an asshole as mine, or if that's just my particular burden. Probably everyone thinks they have it worse. That's another thing we do: assume our suffering is somehow special, more legitimate than others'. It's not, of course. Suffering is democratic. It shows up everywhere.

There's a bird outside my window. I don't know what kind. I'm not good with birds. I never learned. My father could name them all—he was one of those people who knew things about nature. I'm more the type who knows obscure facts about movies or can tell you the history of the sandwich. Useful knowledge for parties, useless knowledge for actual living. That's always been my trade-off. Interesting but impractical.

The coffee in my mug is getting cold. I should drink it or throw it out, but instead I'm watching it. There's something hypnotic about a full mug, the possibilities it contains. In a moment it'll be empty. In an hour it'll be gone entirely. That seems sad for no rational reason. It's just coffee. But isn't that true of most things? We're sad about losing things that are fundamentally replaceable. We're nostalgic for moments that weren't even that good when we were living them. I remember thinking certain Tuesday nights in college were boring. Now I'd do anything to have one back.

I've been wondering about ambition lately. Do I have it? I think I do, but it's strange and sideways. I don't want to be famous or rich, which seems to be the default. I want to make something true. I want to create something that feels inevitable in retrospect—like it had to exist. Of course, there's probably someone doing this very second, probably better than I could. That's the paralyzing part of living now. Everything's already been done. Every joke's been made. Every story's been told. We're all just remixing. But then again, isn't that always how it's been? Shakespeare was remixing too. We just don't think about it because the originals are gone.

There's a conversation happening somewhere that's going to change someone's life. A text message is being written that'll be reread a hundred times. A decision is being made right now that'll echo forward for years. And most of these momentous things feel completely ordinary while they're happening. You don't know you're in a pivotal moment until much later, if ever. How do we live knowing that? How do we treat every conversation like it might be important, when most aren't? I think the answer is: we don't. We can't. We'd go insane. We have to treat most moments as forgettable because they are.

I think about death more than I probably should. Not in a dangerous way—more in a philosophical way. Like, I'll be thinking about whether I want pizza or pasta for dinner, and then suddenly I remember that I'll die, and it seems crazy that I'm worried about pizza. But then the moment passes and I'm back to worrying about pizza. That's the thing about mortality awareness: it doesn't actually change your life. It just occasionally crashes the party and reminds you of the stakes, then leaves. The worrying about dinner resumes.

There's a self-help book somewhere that claims you should write like nobody's reading. Write the truth. Don't perform. But here I am, writing these words into the void, and I'm still performing, aren't I? I'm selecting these words carefully. I'm shaping this narrative. Even in attempted honesty, we're dishonest. We can't help it. We're aesthetic creatures before we're authentic ones.

But maybe that's okay. Maybe the performance is part of being human. We're all playing roles—not in a fake way, but in the sense that we're all presenting a version of ourselves to the world. The version that's convenient, that fits. The version that makes sense to other people. And sometimes, if we're lucky, someone sees the version underneath and doesn't run away. That's probably what love is—just someone looking at the rough draft and saying, "Yeah, that's okay. That's real." Not because it's polished or perfect, but because it's true.

I should probably wrap this up. The page is getting fuller, and I don't want to overstay my welcome in the reader's mind. There's an art to knowing when to stop. To knowing when you've said enough. To editing. But sometimes the best moments come right at the end, the ones you almost cut. And sometimes they don't. Sometimes they're just filler, and you were right to cut them. How do you know the difference? I guess you just have to trust your gut, even when your gut is confused about pizza.

The coffee is definitely cold now. I'm drinking it anyway. It tastes like regret and stubbornness, which is basically my brand. The bird is gone from the window. The light has shifted. It's later than it was before. That's the only guarantee, isn't it? Things keep moving forward whether we're ready or not. Time is the one force we can't negotiate with. No matter how much sense we try to make of it, it just keeps going.

I think that's something.
